course.title: AP U.S. History
course.description: Trace how Americans have argued over identity, power, work, and their place in the world, from the societies that existed before 1491 to the present.
course.previewDescription: Follow the nation's development from early contact and colonization through independence, civil war, industrialization, world wars, and recent decades.

unit.title: Period 5
unit.description: Follow Manifest Destiny and the Mexican–American War, the sectional conflict over slavery, the election of 1860 and secession, the Civil War, and Reconstruction and its failure from 1844 to 1877.

topic.title: Reconstruction
topic.summary: How Presidents Lincoln and Johnson and Congress disagreed over Reconstruction, what the 13th, 14th, and 15th Amendments did, how the women's rights movement split, and what Reconstruction achieved in the South.

framework.name: Course themes
framework.title: Use the course themes to choose your evidence
framework.intro: The themes connect developments across all nine periods. A piece of evidence can fit more than one theme; choose the one that answers the prompt.
framework.sourceNote: Theme names, codes, and descriptions follow the AP U.S. History Course and Exam Description (fall 2026).

themes.title: American and National Identity
themes.description: This theme focuses on how and why definitions of American and national identity and values have developed among the diverse and changing population of North America as well as on related topics, such as citizenship, constitutionalism, foreign policy, assimilation, and American exceptionalism.
themes.question: Who counted as American, and what did people believe the nation stood for?
themes.example: Debates over ratifying the Constitution turned on what kind of republic Americans wanted.

themes.title: Work, Exchange, and Technology
themes.description: This theme focuses on the factors behind the development of systems of economic exchange, particularly the role of technology, economic markets, and government.
themes.question: How did people earn a living, trade, and use new technology?
themes.example: Canals and railroads tied farmers in the West to markets in the East.

themes.title: Geography and the Environment
themes.description: This theme focuses on the role of geography and both the natural and human-made environments in the social and political developments in what would become the United States.
themes.question: How did land, climate, and resources shape choices, and how did people change them?
themes.example: The Chesapeake's climate suited tobacco, which shaped its labor system.

themes.title: Migration and Settlement
themes.description: This theme focuses on why and how the various people who moved to and within the United States both adapted to and transformed their new social and physical environments.
themes.question: Why did people move, and how did they change the places they settled?
themes.example: The Great Migration brought African Americans from the rural South to northern cities.

themes.title: Politics and Power
themes.description: This theme focuses on how different social and political groups have influenced society and government in the United States as well as how political beliefs and institutions have changed over time.
themes.question: Who held power, how did they use it, and who challenged it?
themes.example: The New Deal expanded the federal government's role in the economy.

themes.title: America in the World
themes.description: This theme focuses on the interactions between nations that affected North American history in the colonial period and on the influence of the United States on world affairs.
themes.question: How did contact, trade, diplomacy, and war connect America to other nations?
themes.example: The Seven Years' War left Britain in debt and changed its policies toward the colonies.

themes.title: American and Regional Culture
themes.description: This theme focuses on the how and why national, regional, and group cultures developed and changed as well as how culture has shaped government policy and the economy.
themes.question: How did beliefs, religion, arts, and media develop and shape public life?
themes.example: The Second Great Awakening inspired many Americans to join reform movements.

themes.title: Social Structures
themes.description: This theme focuses on how and why systems of social organization develop and change as well as the impact that these systems have on the broader society.
themes.question: How were people ranked by race, class, and gender, and how did that change?
themes.example: The growth of a middle class in the Gilded Age changed ideas about leisure and family.

questions.prompt: Lincoln's Ten Percent Plan of 1863 proposed that
choices: a state could return only after a majority of its voters had taken an oath of loyalty
a state could return once ten percent of its voters took a loyalty oath
former Confederate leaders be tried for treason and their land given to freed people
the army govern the Southern states for a decade before any state could return
questions.explanation: Lincoln wanted to restore the Southern states quickly, and he asked only a small share of voters to accept the Union and the end of slavery.
choiceExplanations: That was the requirement of the Wade–Davis Bill.
Lincoln wanted to restore the Southern states quickly, and he asked only a small share of voters to accept the Union and the end of slavery.
The plan was lenient and did not seize land.
That described Congress's later plan.
questions.distinguisher: The majority oath choice is close because it was also a loyalty oath, but it was the requirement of the stricter Wade–Davis Bill.
questions.subskillText: Identify a historical concept, development, or process.

questions.prompt: The Black Codes passed by Southern states in 1865 and 1866
choices: gave freed people the right to vote and to hold office in the Southern states
were federal laws that protected the property of freed people in the South
required the Northern states to return people who had escaped slavery
limited the freedom of freed people, such as their work and movement
questions.explanation: The Codes tried to keep Black workers on the plantations under conditions close to slavery, and they angered Northerners.
choiceExplanations: The Codes denied political rights.
They were state laws and they restricted freed people.
They concerned the former slave states.
The Codes tried to keep Black workers on the plantations under conditions close to slavery, and they angered Northerners.
questions.distinguisher: The right to vote choice is close because Reconstruction later brought the vote to Black men, but the Codes aimed to deny it.
questions.subskillText: Explain a historical concept, development, or process.

questions.prompt: Which of the following helps to explain why Congress passed the Reconstruction Acts of 1867?
choices: Southern governments had passed Black Codes and elected former Confederate leaders
President Johnson had asked Congress to take control of the process of Reconstruction
The Supreme Court had ordered the army to occupy the Southern states
Northern states had demanded that the South pay the cost of the war
questions.explanation: Many Republicans believed that Johnson's plan had returned power to the old leaders without protecting the freed people.
choiceExplanations: Many Republicans believed that Johnson's plan had returned power to the old leaders without protecting the freed people.
Johnson opposed the Acts and vetoed them.
Congress acted before the Court did.
The Acts concerned rights and government.
questions.distinguisher: The Johnson request choice is close because the president had a role in Reconstruction, but he opposed the Acts and Congress passed them over his veto.
questions.subskillText: Explain how a historical development or process relates to another historical development or process.

choices: gave African American men the right to vote throughout the nation
abolished slavery in every part of the United States
made all persons born in the United States citizens
gave women the right to vote in elections for federal office
questions.explanation: The Amendment overturned the Dred Scott ruling on citizenship and set a standard of equal protection for all persons.
choiceExplanations: That was the Fifteenth Amendment.
That was the Thirteenth Amendment.
The Amendment overturned the Dred Scott ruling on citizenship and set a standard of equal protection for all persons.
That was the Nineteenth Amendment of 1920.
questions.distinguisher: The right to vote choice is close because the three amendments are often taught together, but the Fifteenth Amendment dealt with voting.
questions.subskillText: Identify a historical concept, development, or process.

questions.prompt: The Fifteenth Amendment (1870) barred the denial of the vote
choices: on account of sex, which opened the vote to all adult women
to men who could not read, which ended the use of literacy tests
to men who owned no property, which ended property requirements
on account of race, color, or previous condition of servitude
questions.explanation: The Amendment aimed to protect the vote of Black men, but it left room for states to use other tests.
choiceExplanations: The amendment did not mention sex.
The Amendment did not ban such tests.
Most states had already dropped those requirements.
The Amendment aimed to protect the vote of Black men, but it left room for states to use other tests.
questions.distinguisher: The sex choice is close because women's suffrage leaders wanted it included, but the Amendment did not mention sex.
questions.subskillText: Explain a historical concept, development, or process.

questions.prompt: Why did Elizabeth Cady Stanton and Susan B. Anthony oppose the Fifteenth Amendment?
choices: It denied Black men the right to vote in the states of the North
It extended the vote to Black men but not to women
It required women to pay a poll tax before they could vote
It gave the vote to immigrants before it gave the vote to women
questions.explanation: Stanton and Anthony had worked for both causes and were disappointed that the amendment did not include women.
choiceExplanations: It protected the vote of Black men.
Stanton and Anthony had worked for both causes and were disappointed that the amendment did not include women.
It did not mention women or taxes.
It concerned race and not immigration.
questions.distinguisher: The Black men choice is close because they were concerned with Black rights, but they had favored them and objected to the omission of women.
questions.subskillText: Explain how a historical development or process relates to another historical development or process.

questions.prompt: Which of the following describes a difference between Johnson's Reconstruction and Congressional Reconstruction after 1867?
choices: Johnson let the South return with few conditions, and Congress imposed army rule
Johnson required Black men to vote in the South, and Congress forbade their voting
Johnson punished Confederate leaders harshly, and Congress pardoned all of them
Johnson ruled the South by the army, and Congress returned it to civilian rule
questions.explanation: Johnson's plan restored the Southern governments quickly, while the Reconstruction Acts placed the South under the army and required Black suffrage.
choiceExplanations: Johnson's plan restored the Southern governments quickly, while the Reconstruction Acts placed the South under the army and required Black suffrage.
The positions are reversed.
Johnson pardoned most Confederates.
Congress set up military districts.
questions.distinguisher: The reversed choice is close because both plans dealt with Black voting, but Johnson opposed it and Congress required it.
questions.subskillText: Identify patterns among or connections between historical developments and processes.

questions.prompt: Which of the following was a political opportunity opened to African Americans during Reconstruction?
choices: Black men held a majority of the seats in every Southern state legislature
Black women won the right to vote in elections in the Southern states
Black men voted and held office, including seats in Congress
Black Southerners gained control of the federal courts in the Southern states
questions.explanation: Black voters elected Black officials, such as Hiram Revels, who served in the Senate from Mississippi.
choiceExplanations: That was true in only a few states, and for a short time.
Women did not vote in this period.
Black voters elected Black officials, such as Hiram Revels, who served in the Senate from Mississippi.
Federal judges were appointed by the president.
questions.distinguisher: The majority of seats choice is close because Black officeholders were numerous in some states, but they did not hold a majority in every one.
questions.subskillText: Identify a historical concept, development, or process.

questions.prompt: The impeachment of Andrew Johnson in 1868 is best understood in the context of which of the following?
choices: A charge that Johnson had helped to plan the assassination of Lincoln
A dispute between Johnson and Congress over the purchase of Alaska
A decision by the Supreme Court that Johnson had broken the Constitution
A struggle between Congress and the president over how to carry out Reconstruction
questions.explanation: Radical Republicans in Congress clashed with Johnson over the Reconstruction Acts and the Tenure of Office Act, and the House voted to impeach him.
choiceExplanations: No such charge was made.
Johnson's administration purchased Alaska in 1867.
The Supreme Court played no part.
Radical Republicans in Congress clashed with Johnson over the Reconstruction Acts and the Tenure of Office Act, and the House voted to impeach him.
questions.distinguisher: The assassination choice is close because Johnson came to office after Lincoln's death, but the impeachment concerned his conflict with Congress.
questions.subskillText: Identify and describe a historical context for a specific historical development or process.

questions.prompt: Which of the following statements about the amendments is best supported by the table?
choices: The amendments gave equal rights in practice to all of the nation's people
Each amendment left some question of rights unsettled or open to evasion
The amendments were ratified in an order opposite to their numbers
All three amendments applied only to the states that had joined the Confederacy
questions.explanation: The last column lists a gap for each amendment: forced labor for crime, the limits of the vote, and the omission of women.
choiceExplanations: The right-hand column lists gaps that remained.
The last column lists a gap for each amendment: forced labor for crime, the limits of the vote, and the omission of women.
They were ratified in 1865, 1868, and 1870.
The table describes national rules.
questions.distinguisher: The equal rights choice is close because the amendments did extend rights, but the table shows what each one left open.

questions.prompt: Which detail in the table best supports the claim that the amendments divided the women's rights movement?
choices: The Thirteenth Amendment allowed forced labor as a punishment for crime
The Fifteenth Amendment was ratified in 1870, five years after the Thirteenth
The Fourteenth Amendment made all persons born in the nation citizens
The Fourteenth Amendment wrote “male” into the Constitution
questions.explanation: Women's suffrage leaders disagreed about whether to support amendments that gave the vote to Black men and left out women.
choiceExplanations: That detail concerns slavery and crime.
A date does not show a division.
That detail does not concern women's voting.
Women's suffrage leaders disagreed about whether to support amendments that gave the vote to Black men and left out women.
questions.distinguisher: The Thirteenth Amendment choice is close because it is another detail in the table, but it concerns forced labor and not the vote.

questions.prompt: The exception in the Thirteenth Amendment for punishment for crime contributed most directly to which development?
choices: Southern laws that made minor offenses crimes and forced freed people to work
The creation of the Freedmen's Bureau to help the freed people
The passage of the Civil Rights Act of 1866 over Johnson's veto
The impeachment of Johnson by the House of Representatives in 1868
questions.explanation: The Black Codes and later convict labor used the exception to hold freed people to forced work.
choiceExplanations: The Black Codes and later convict labor used the exception to hold freed people to forced work.
The Bureau was created to help them.
The Act protected the freed people.
That event concerned the president and Congress.
questions.distinguisher: The Civil Rights Act choice is close because it responded to the Black Codes, but it was a reaction to them and not an effect of the exception.
